title: Nehemiah
subtitle: The walls of Jerusalem rebuilt and the covenant renewed
lead: Nehemiah is the story of a Jewish official at the Persian court who hears that Jerusalem's walls lie broken, weeps and prays, and gets the king's leave to go and rebuild them. Much of it is told in his own words. He inspects the ruins by night, organizes the whole people into building teams, and finishes the wall in fifty-two days, while neighboring leaders mock, threaten and plot against him, and while the poor cry out against Jews who are taking their land and their children for debt.

The second half turns from stones to people. Ezra reads the law of Moses to the assembled people, who weep, celebrate the Feast of Booths, confess their sins and sign a written pledge to keep the law. Jerusalem is filled with settlers, the wall is dedicated with two great choirs, and Nehemiah, back from the king years later, angrily puts right what has slipped: the Temple storeroom, the tithes, the Sabbath and marriages with foreigners. The book ends with his prayer, "My God, remember me for good."
facts: Not named as a whole. Large parts are Nehemiah's own memoir in the first person (1:1–7:5; parts of 12:27–43; 13:4–31). Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): Ezra wrote the book of Ezra–Nehemiah and Nehemiah finished it. Most scholars see an unnamed editor who joined Nehemiah's memoir to lists and to the Ezra story of chapters 8–10. Most scholars now think a different hand from Chronicles; some still argue for a common author or school.

Written after the events: most scholars say about 400–300 BC for the finished book, with Nehemiah's memoir written soon after 433 BC. Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (2:1), almost always taken as Artaxerxes I, so 445 BC (444 on one reckoning). He governs twelve years (5:14), returns to the king in 433 BC, and comes back some time later (13:6–7).
Susa, the Persian winter capital, and Jerusalem, a thinly settled city in the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud), ringed by rival leaders in Samaria, Ammon, Arabia and Ashdod.

Historical narrative built around a first-person memoir and documents: prayers (1:5–11; 9:5–37), a list of builders (3), the list of returnees (7:6–73, nearly the same as Ezra 2), a signed pledge (9:38–10:39), lists of settlers, priests and Levites (11–12), and short "remember me" prayers (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31).

13 chapters, 406 verses. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, called Ezra; the Masoretes counted their verses together and marked the middle of the book at 3:32. Hebrew numbering differs at 4:1–23 (Hebrew 3:33–4:17) and 9:38–10:39 (Hebrew 10:1–40). The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) puts Ezra–Nehemiah just before Chronicles at the end of the Bible, and most printed Hebrew Bibles, like the Talmud, end with Chronicles; the Aleppo and Leningrad codices put Chronicles first among the Writings and Ezra–Nehemiah last, so the Bible ends with Nehemiah. Christian Bibles place it after Ezra among the histories.
authorship: The Talmud says Ezra wrote his book and that Nehemiah son of Hacaliah finished it (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), treating Ezra–Nehemiah as one book. On this view the first-person chapters (1:1–7:5; 12:27–43; 13:4–31) are Nehemiah's own words, and the lists and the story of Ezra's reading (8–10) were joined to them by Nehemiah or in his lifetime. The memoir's vivid detail, its exact dates and its frankness about enemies and failures fit a writer who lived through the events.
Critical scholarship: a memoir set in a larger book

Almost all scholars accept that the Nehemiah memoir is genuine, one of the few first-person writings by a known person in the Hebrew Bible, written soon after 433 BC (5:14). They debate its purpose: a report to the Persian king, a defense against critics in Judah, or an account laid before God like a votive or memorial inscription, as the "remember me" prayers suggest (Mowinckel and von Rad; Kellermann read it instead as an accused man's prayer; Williamson surveys the views). An editor, most say about 400–300 BC, combined it with lists (3; 7; 10–12) and with the Ezra story of chapters 8–10, which some scholars think once followed Ezra 8; 1 Esdras places the reading of the law directly after Ezra 10 (1 Esdras 9:37–55). The priestly list runs to Jaddua (12:11, 22), whom many place late in the Persian period. Jacob Wright argues that the memoir itself grew in stages as later writers added to it.

Since Leopold Zunz (1832), many held that one "Chronicler" wrote Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah as one history. Sara Japhet (1968) and H. G. M. Williamson (1977) argued from language and ideas that Chronicles is a separate work, and most scholars now agree, though some, such as Blenkinsopp, still argue for a common author or school. This site treats Ezra–Nehemiah as one work in two books, as Ezra's opening pages do.

audience.to: The Jewish community of the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud) and its Temple in Jerusalem, probably some generations after Nehemiah, in the late Persian or early Greek period (about 400–300 BC), and behind the memoir, Nehemiah's own first readers: the people of Jerusalem and, before them, God himself, whom his "remember me" prayers address. They lived in a walled but thinly settled city, ruled by a foreign empire, short of money and land, and divided from neighbors in Samaria and Ammon who claimed a say in Jerusalem.
audience.why: To show them that their city and its walls, its Temple worship and its way of life under the law had been restored by God's "good hand" through a faithful leader, against opposition from outside and greed inside, and that the people as a whole had bound themselves by oath to keep the law. Knowing this audience explains the book's lists of builders and families (who belongs, and who did the work), its stress on the Sabbath, tithes and marriage (the boundaries that kept a small people distinct), its frank picture of rich Jews exploiting poor ones, and Nehemiah's habit of turning to God in short prayers: the memoir asks God, and readers, to judge his record.
views: Traditional readers, following the Talmud, hold that Nehemiah wrote or finished the book in his own lifetime, about 430–400 BC, to record how God restored Jerusalem and to call the community to keep its pledge.
A memoir set in a later book

Most critical scholars think Nehemiah wrote his memoir soon after 433 BC, perhaps as a report to the king, a defense against critics, or a votive account set before God in the Temple, and that an editor about 400–300 BC built it into Ezra–Nehemiah for a later community. Some see that editor shaping the story to give the reforms of Ezra first place (chapters 8–10).

Those who hold that the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah read the books together as one history from Adam to Nehemiah, written for Temple circles in Jerusalem; most scholars since Japhet and Williamson read them as separate works with different emphases.

outline: News of Jerusalem's ruin reaches Nehemiah at Susa; his prayer
Leave from Artaxerxes; the journey, the night inspection and the call to build
The builders of the wall, gate by gate
Mockery, a plot and a guard; building with weapons in hand
The outcry of the poor, the debts cancelled, and Nehemiah's record as governor
Plots against Nehemiah; the wall finished in fifty-two days
The city guarded; the register of those who first came back
Ezra reads the law; the Feast of Booths
A day of confession and the Levites' great prayer
The signed pledge to keep the law
Jerusalem resettled by lot; the towns of Judah and Benjamin
Priests and Levites; the dedication of the wall with two choirs
Nehemiah's second term: the Temple room, tithes, the Sabbath and mixed marriages

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Nehemiah is a true account of the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, told largely in Nehemiah's own words. The Talmud counts Ezra and Nehemiah as one book and says Nehemiah finished it (Bava Batra 15a).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars see Nehemiah's first-person memoir (1–7, parts of 12–13) as one of the most reliable sources for Persian-period Judah, set beside lists and an Ezra story (8–10) by a later editor. They debate the order of Ezra and Nehemiah and how the book's parts were joined.

lenses.name: Persian records
lenses.desc: Nehemiah served at the Persian court in Susa, and his opponents appear outside the Bible: the Elephantine papyri name Sanballat as governor of Samaria and the high priest Johanan (12:22–23), a silver bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta names "Qaynu son of Geshem, king of Qedar", and the name Tobiah is carved at 'Araq el-Emir in Jordan, the later seat of the Tobiad family (the inscription is usually dated centuries after Nehemiah).

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis honor Nehemiah as a builder and reformer but fault him for praising himself ('My God, remember me for good'; Sanhedrin 93b). The public reading of the Torah in chapter 8 is taken as the model for synagogue reading and for explaining the text in translation (Megillah 3a).

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Christians read the rebuilt walls and the renewed covenant as part of God's faithfulness after exile, and Nehemiah as a model of prayer and leadership. The decree to rebuild Jerusalem (2:1–8) is one starting point often used to count Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:25).

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site and the book of Ezra: YHWH is "the LORD"; hesed is "loyal love"; netinim are "the temple servants"; the province west of the Euphrates is "Beyond the River"; the high priest is "the high priest"; Nehemiah's prayer zochrah li elohay letovah is "My God, remember me for good" at both 5:19 and 13:31; and seganim are "deputies" throughout Ezra and Nehemiah. Gate and place names follow one list across the book (the Sheep Gate, the Fish Gate, the Jeshanah Gate, the Valley Gate, the Dung Gate, the Spring Gate, the Water Gate, the Horse Gate, the East Gate, the Miphkad Gate; Serpent Spring; the bend in the wall).

Verse numbers

This site uses the English verse numbers. Hebrew Bibles number 4:1–6 as 3:33–38 and 4:7–23 as 4:1–17, and 9:38 as 10:1, with chapter 10 one verse higher throughout. In chapter 7, Hebrew Bibles lack verse 68 (see the variant) and number 7:69–73 as 7:68–72.

The list in chapter 7

Nehemiah 7:6–73 is nearly the same list as Ezra 2. Where the Hebrew is the same, the Plain English Translation uses the site's Ezra 2 wording exactly; where it differs, in names, numbers and small words, the English differs too, and the chapter page has a table of the differences.

The text and the Greek

The Plain English Translation follows the Leningrad Codex. Where the Masoretes mark a reading to be read aloud (Qere) in place of the written text (Ketiv), the Plain English Translation follows the Qere, except in names where the written form has other support (the Greek or a parallel list), unless a parallel list in the book itself shows the Qere's name is meant (as at 12:16); the variants give every pair that changes a name or the English. In chapters 1–7 the Plain English Translation departs from the Leningrad Codex only at 7:68, a verse missing from it, and follows the Ketiv only at 3:20 (Zabbai). In chapters 8–13 it follows the Ketiv at 10:19 (Nobai) and 12:14 (Malluchi) and the Qere elsewhere, including the name Iddo at 12:16. The Greek 2 Esdras (Esdras B), in which Nehemiah is chapters 11–23, is a close translation; where this site cites it, the reading was checked in Rahlfs' text as printed online at die-bibel.de. 1 Esdras has no parallel to Nehemiah 1–7 except the list of 7:6–73, which it gives in its Ezra 2 form (1 Esdras 5:7–46). It also has the reading of the law (7:73–8:12), placed straight after the marriage reform of Ezra 10 (1 Esdras 9:37–55).

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has two halves. Chapters 1–7 are Nehemiah's memoir of the rebuilding: the news and prayer at Susa (1), the king's permission and the night inspection (2), the list of builders (3), opposition and armed building (4), the debt crisis (5), plots against Nehemiah and the finished wall (6), and the guarding and enrolling of the city (7). Chapters 8–13 turn from walls to people: Ezra's reading of the law and the Feast of Booths (8), a great prayer of confession (9), a signed pledge (10), the resettlement of Jerusalem and lists of priests and Levites (11–12), the dedication of the wall (12:27–47), and Nehemiah's reforms on a second visit (13). The register of chapter 7 is the hinge: the same list that began the return in Ezra 2 now closes the building of the walls and opens the renewal of the covenant.

In the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, called Ezra. The Talmud treats them so (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a), and the Masoretes counted their verses together, placing the middle of the book at Nehemiah 3:32. Origen and Jerome knew the division into two, and Jerome's Latin Bible called them 1 and 2 Esdras; in the Greek, Nehemiah is the second half of 2 Esdras. Hebrew Bibles adopted the division only in the late Middle Ages. In the Talmud's order the book comes just before Chronicles at the end of the Writings. In the Aleppo and Leningrad codices, which this site follows, Chronicles comes first among the Writings and Ezra–Nehemiah last, so the Bible ends with Nehemiah's "remember me for good." Christian Bibles, following the Greek, place Ezra and Nehemiah after Chronicles among the histories.

sections.h: Dates, and Ezra or Nehemiah first?
sections.b:
Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (2:1), governed twelve years, to the thirty-second year (5:14; 13:6), went back to the king and returned some time later (13:6–7). Almost all scholars identify the king as Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC), which gives 445–433 BC for the first term; an Elephantine letter of 407 BC naming the sons of Sanballat and the high priest Johanan supports this. On the usual reckoning the news came in Kislev 446 BC and the audience in Nisan 445 BC; Harold Hoehner, counting the king's years from Tishri, puts them in 445 and 444 BC (see the chapter 1 page).

Ezra, the book says, came in the seventh year of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:7–8). The traditional order, Ezra in 458 BC and Nehemiah in 445 BC, is how the books present it, with the two men together at the reading of the law and the dedication of the wall (8:9; 12:26; 12:36). Some scholars put Ezra under Artaxerxes II, in 398 BC, after Nehemiah, because Nehemiah's memoir rarely mentions Ezra, the Jehohanan son of Eliashib whose room Ezra used (Ezra 10:6), if he is the later high priest Johanan (12:22), would be the grandson of Nehemiah's Eliashib (12:10–11), and Ezra seems to find a walled and peopled city (Ezra 9:9; Ezra 10:1). Others emend Ezra 7:7 to the thirty-seventh year (428 BC), so that the two overlap. Williamson and many others defend the traditional order; the question remains open.

Praised as a reformer. Ben Sira honors him as the one who "raised our fallen walls" (Sirach 49:13). 2 Maccabees credits him with rebuilding the Temple and altar and collecting the books of the kings and prophets (2 Maccabees 1:18–36; 2 Maccabees 2:13). Christian writers have long held him up as a model of prayer, courage and leadership, and modern leadership books often use chapters 1–6.

Criticized for self-praise and harshness. The Talmud asks why the book was not called by his name, and answers that he took credit to himself ("My God, remember me for good") and spoke badly of the governors before him (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). In chapter 13 he beats and curses men who married foreign women and pulls out their hair (13:25), and expels the high priest's grandson (13:28). David Clines and others read the memoir as skilled self-justification, to be weighed rather than simply believed.

Both together. Many readers see a leader of real courage and justice, who defended the poor against his own class (5), and who was also hard, sure of himself and quick to anger. The memoir gives his side of events; the site presents each reading and lets readers weigh the record.

Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem are known or probably known from outside the Bible (see the A lens). The memoir presents them as enemies of God's work, mocking, plotting and hiring prophets. Many historians add that they were the established leaders of Samaria, Ammon and the Arabs of Qedar, linked to Jerusalem by marriage, worship of the LORD and trade, who had reason to fear a walled city under a governor with royal backing. The book itself gives them no voice beyond their taunts and letters. Readers can hold both truths: their interests were real, and from the book's point of view they stood against what God was doing.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read Nehemiah
sections.b:
In Jewish tradition, the reading of the law in Nehemiah 8 is the model for public Torah reading with explanation (Bavli Megillah 3a), and the pledge of chapter 10 and the Sabbath reforms of chapter 13 shaped later Jewish practice. Nehemiah himself is honored as a builder of Jerusalem, though the rabbis criticized his self-praise. Jewish tradition counts Daniel's seventy weeks not from Nehemiah 2 but from the First Temple's fall to the Second's (Seder Olam; Rashi); on ordinary dates 586 BC to AD 70 is 656 years, and the rabbinic chronology reaches 490 by giving the Persian period only 34 years, while Cyrus's decree, another starting point, concerns the Temple (Ezra 1:2–4), not the city. The book's last place in the Leningrad Codex makes "remember me for good" the final words of the Hebrew Bible in that order.

Christians read Nehemiah as part of God's faithfulness after exile, leading to the Jerusalem and Temple of Jesus' day. Many count Daniel's seventy weeks from 2:1–8. Preachers have used the rebuilding of the walls as a picture of the church built up by every member, and Nehemiah's prayers as a model. The confession of chapter 9 is one of the great summaries of Israel's history in the Bible.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book about the city's boundaries
spec.body: My own reading: Nehemiah is a book about boundaries. Chapters 1–7 build a physical boundary, a wall with doors and guards. Chapters 8–13 build the boundaries of a people: who hears the law, who signs the pledge, who lives inside the walls, who may enter the Temple's rooms, which days are holy, whom one may marry. The same verbs and images cross over: gates are shut against Sabbath traders as they were shut against enemies (7:3; 13:19), and Tobiah is thrown out of a Temple room as he was shut out of Jerusalem (2:20; 13:8). Many scholars stress the theme of separation in Ezra–Nehemiah (Eskenazi; Williamson; Blenkinsopp), Eskenazi argues that holiness spreads from the Temple to the whole city, and Jacob Wright's Rebuilding Identity (2004) reads the building account as the core from which the book's later layers grew; reading the wall-building as the pattern for every later reform is my own suggestion, and it helps explain why the book keeps the story of the stones and the story of the covenant together.

Beside the king sits a queen with a veil and a lotus flower. Servants with trays stand behind. Lamps glow; through a doorway the night sky shows.

reading: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah (Word Biblical Commentary, 1985)
The standard detailed commentary, careful on the memoir, the lists and the history.
A critical commentary attentive to social conflict and the book's sources.
F. Charles Fensham, The Books of Ezra and Nehemiah (NICOT, 1982)
An evangelical commentary strong on the Persian background.
A short, clear evangelical commentary with good notes on chronology.
Tamara Cohn Eskenazi, In an Age of Prose (1988)
A literary reading of Ezra–Nehemiah as the story of a whole community.
Jacob L. Wright, Rebuilding Identity: The Nehemiah-Memoir and Its Earliest Readers (2004)
A study of how the memoir grew and what it meant to its first readers.
Edwin M. Yamauchi, Persia and the Bible (1990)
The Persian world of Susa, the court and the empire, for the background.
